summary: The source contract limits word length to at most five and fixes the alphabet at 26 letters, so neighbor generation has constant legal work per dictionary word. Reading the dictionary and writing all R returned word positions already require Omega(N + R) time.

optimality.argument: In the worst case, an uninspected dictionary word can add a shortest route or be the missing link to the target, so exact enumeration requires Omega(N) dictionary inspection. Materializing the requested sequences requires another Omega(R), where R is the total number of word positions across all returned sequences. Because legal words contain at most five letters over a fixed 26-letter alphabet, the candidate tries at most 125 constant-length substitutions per visited word. Its BFS, bounded-degree parent DAG, and backtracking therefore take O(N + R) time.

replacement_checks.evidence: An unseen dictionary word can create an additional shortest sequence, while every one of the R returned word positions must be written.
With L <= 5 and a fixed 26-letter alphabet, each visited word produces at most 125 constant-size candidate substitutions; backtracking performs work proportional to the returned sequences.
The source-fidelity-verified examples cover multiple shortest sequences and an absent target; black-box real-test execution verifies every existing ordinary check without inspecting its definition.
